newsitem.title: FRANCE: TENNIS-GRAF MAINTAINS FRENCH OPEN SEQUENCE.
newsitem.headline: TENNIS-GRAF MAINTAINS FRENCH OPEN SEQUENCE.

text.p: Steffi Graf stepped briskly back into French Open action on Tuesday to safeguard her remarkable first round record at Roland Garros with a 6-1 6-4 victory over Argentine Paola Suarez.
It was Graf's 15th successive first round win in Paris without dropping a set, dating all the way back to 1983 when she recorded her first Grand Slam singles victory at the tender age of 13.
Yet, like many of its predecessors, the 54-minute runabout was not so much a contest as an opportunity for veteran Graf-watchers to gauge the mood of a woman with plenty on her mind.

Only France's Mary Pierce has managed to beat Graf on Parisian clay since her dramatic final defeat to Monica Seles in 1992 but locker-room talk suggests the former world number one is more vulnerable than usual this time.

A crushing 6-0 6-1 defeat to South African Amanda Coetzer in Berlin earlier this month, added to tendinitis in her left knee, has certainly removed the aura of invincibility which used to surround her.

The simultaneous rise of Martina Hingis has also presented a fresh threat but, despite a sloppy second set against Suarez in which she lost three successive games from 5-1 to 5-4, Graf believes she is still a force to be reckoned with.

"I felt very good out there and I served a lot stronger than in Strasbourg last week. Until the end I didn't really make too many mistakes," said the German, who spent three months away from the court between February and the beginning of May.
To her surprise, she found the break more enjoyable than she anticipated. "It gave me some time away from everything. I haven't had that sort of time away from tennis for a long time."
Even so, Graf's commitment to her day job remains absolute. She was among the earliest arrivals at the practice courts on Tuesday and continues to run a shrewd eye over her potential rivals.
She personally believes Jana Novotna "should not be under-estimated" but side-stepped predictions about her own chances of a sixth French title.
"It's easier to say after two or three rounds when you see how the others are playing," she said.
In the men's singles, ninth seed Carlos Moya's unfinished match against fellow Spaniard Alberto Martin, level at two sets all overnight, was settled in 37 minutes on another sunny day.
Moya won the decisive set 6-3, the crucial break arriving in the sixth game when Martin saved five break points only to hit a forehand long to lose the sixth.
